title: Holding your hem
hookLine: leaving praise and blame, I have caught hold of Your hem, sung as the couple takes the scarf (Ramkali ki Var M5, ang 963)

lines: A SCARF OVER THE GROOM'S SHOULDER.
cards: Before the four rounds begin, there's a small gesture that's easy to miss. The groom has a long scarf over his shoulder. The bride's father stands, takes one end of it, and places it in his daughter's hand.
Nobody makes a speech. But the musicians are singing a line as it happens, and if you know the words, the gesture changes. Because the line isn't about the groom at all.

teach.b: The scarf is called the palla. The shabad sung as it's placed comes from Guru Arjan's Var in Raag Ramkali, on Ang nine sixty-three.

In paraphrase: praise and slander, I have given them all up; I have let everything go. I have seen that all relationships are false, so I have caught hold of Your hem. It's startling to sing at a wedding.
All relationships are false? On the day two families join? But the singer isn't the bride speaking to the groom.
In Gurbani the soul is often the bride and God the Husband. The one whose hem she grabs is the Lord.
So the shabad reminds everyone in the room of something tender and a little fierce: the deepest thing to hold on to, it says, isn't another person, even this beloved person. It's the One.

teach.h: TWO WHO EACH HOLD ON TO GOD.
teach.b: One reading draws a lesson for the marriage too: two people who each hold God's hem aren't asking each other to be everything. Then look at what's let go first: praise and slander, ustat and nindaa.
What people say about you, good or bad. A wedding is full of it: the clothes, the food, the gossip about the in-laws. The shabad drops all of it before the first step.
The palla itself is just cloth. But held in a bride's hand, with that line in the air, it becomes a picture of a soul taking hold of what won't let go.
The couple walks the four rounds holding it, so neither walks alone.

how: At an Anand Karaj, while the bride's father places one end of the groom's palla in her hand, ragis sing Guru Arjan's line about letting go of praise and slander and holding the Lord's hem.

o: the groom's turban, tied for the day
a scarf's end, the hem you hold

games.q: the scarf and the hem — tap the pairs.
p: places the scarf in her hand

s: the line sung at the palla is the bride speaking to the groom
the soul is the bride, and the hem she holds is the Lord's.
the shabad lets go of both praise and slander
ustat and nindaa: what people say, good or bad, is given up first.

games.q: the musicians sing, 'I have caught hold of Your hem.' whose hem does the shabad mean?
games.why: in Gurbani the soul is the bride and God the Husband: the hem is the Lord's, even as the bride holds the groom's scarf.

practice: If someone you love is near, take their hand for a moment; if not, hold your own hands together, or something that belongs to someone you love, a scarf, a ring, a photo, and feel the simple fact of holding on.
Then gently let go of one thing people say about you, good or bad, that you've been carrying. If you pray, say Waheguru as you hold.

wordCard.voice: Palla, the end of a scarf, a hem: Guru Arjan's line, sung as the bride takes it, lets go of praise and slander, as the soul catches hold of the Lord's hem.

orig.note: Punjabi: the end of a scarf, a hem; the palla joins the couple through the four rounds.

carryVoice: Your line: holding the hem. Praise and slander can both be set down. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var Mahalla 5, salok (ustat nindaa naanak jee mai habh vanjaaee), Ang 963
